# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

NELL experienced her “good” summer, taking full delight in it. She together with Isolde spent nearly all their time outside, taking immense pleasure in every joy provided by Linger Lane, the Nymph’s Well, Reedmere, and Victoria Island. Nell’s wandering habits met with no opposition from Thirza. Early in the vacation, during an afternoon visit to a patient's home, Nell encountered the Tullyvale doctor who had previously attended Posy Fay on the night she suffered from croup; he scrutinized Nell intently, pursed his lips, shook his head, and dispatched a message to Thirza Abernethy through a third party. The message ran:
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0000 }

“Make sure your redheaded girl stays outdoors all through the summer and forbid her from reading books until her step becomes livelier.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0001 }

This communication alarmed Thirza in a healthy manner. Within it, she discerned the fatal sentence of consumption for Nell if it were not meticulously followed. Consequently, Nell experienced the premier golden summer of her existence regarding liberty and play. She went on walks, rowed boats, gathered berries, and fantasized as much as her heart desired; and upon September's arrival, she possessed bright eyes and alertness, along with a stride that would have pleased the physician from Tullyvale and a mind filled with renewed drive and enthusiasm.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0002 }

“I am eager to apply myself to my studies with all my energy,” she announced while carrying her volumes down from the garret. “Oh, my dear old companions, seeing your faithful visages again brings me such joy—indeed, geometry, that includes you too. Thirza, my summer was absolutely wonderful, and at present I am exulting like a mighty warrior setting out on a contest, to borrow Mr. Wace’s phrase from this past Sunday. Is Mr. Wace not delivering truly grand discourses? Mrs. Sowerby claims his abilities are growing daily, and before we realize it, a metropolitan congregation will snatch him away, leaving us behind to begin anew with educating yet another inexperienced pastor. However, I fail to understand the point of anticipating misfortune, wouldn't you agree, Thirza? It seems far preferable to simply appreciate Mr. Wace during the time he remains with us. Were I a man, my choice would be to join the clergy. Provided their doctrine is orthodox, they possess the capacity to exert a immense power for righteousness; furthermore, delivering powerful discourses and moving the emotions of your congregation must be exhilarating. Thirza, what prevents women from becoming pastors? Upon putting that query to Mrs. Sowerby, she expressed outrage, declaring that such a practice would be disgraceful. While acknowledging that female clergy might exist in the States—and expressing her belief that they did—she thanked heaven that Canada had not reached such a state, expressing her desire that we never should. Still, the reason eludes me. Women, in my view, would prove to be marvelous pastors. Whenever an event requires organizing, whether a social or a church tea or any other fundraiser, it falls upon the women to step up and perform the labor. Mrs. Sowerby is certainly capable of offering prayers just as effectively as Superintendent Bell, and given a bit of experience, she could undoubtedly deliver sermons as well.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0003 }

“Yes, I think she would be capable of it,” Thirza remarked dryly. “Even now, she engages in a great deal of informal preaching. With Agatha monitoring everyone in Brierley, hardly anyone gets the opportunity to stray.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0004 }

“Thirza,” Nell said, suddenly sharing her feelings, “there is something I want to tell you and get your opinion on. I have been terribly worried by it—specifically on Sunday afternoons, which is when I think about these things in particular. Being good is something I truly want; furthermore, whenever I am around you, Mrs. Wace, or Miss Thorne, I desire it even more, and I wish to do exactly what would make you happy and gain your approval. On the other hand, whenever I am around Mrs. Sowerby, I usually feel exceedingly wicked, experiencing an urge to go and commit the exact act she says I should not do. Doing it becomes an irresistible temptation for me. So, why do you suppose I have those feelings? Could it be that I feel this way because I am genuinely evil and unregenerate?”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0005 }

Thirza appeared doubtful briefly. Afterward, she chuckled.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0006 }

“If that applies to you, Nell, I suppose it applies to me as well, because Agatha frequently impacts me in that exact way. It seems to me at times that her capacity to inspire good, as you put it, would be greater if she refrained from constantly pushing folks to act properly. Nagging ought to have been forbidden by its own distinct commandment. Nevertheless, I ought not to speak in that manner. A pious Christian woman, Agatha possesses good intentions. No one in Brierley has a kinder heart, and she always performs her full portion of labor.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0007 }

“Your agreement gives me immense satisfaction,” Nell stated with conviction. “Such support provides great comfort, and I will be far less anxious about that matter from now on. Nevertheless, I expect different problems will arise to cause me distress. Fresh difficulties appear constantly—matters that confuse a person, as you are aware. The moment one issue is resolved, another immediately takes its place. Entering adulthood requires so many matters to be weighed and determined. I am perpetually occupied with pondering these issues and determining the proper course. Maturing is a solemn affair, is it not, Thirza? Still, possessing such wonderful companions as yourself, Obed, Mrs. Wace, and Miss Thorne means my transition to adulthood should succeed, and failing to do so will certainly be my own doing. The fact that I receive just a single attempt makes it a heavy burden to bear. Should I fail to mature properly, returning to the start for a second try is impossible. My height increased by two inches over the course of this summer, Thirza. At the gathering held by Opal, I was measured by Mr. Pettigrew. Having my recent dresses lengthened by you brings me such joy. The deep-green garment looks lovely, and adding that flounce was a delightful gesture on your part. Naturally, I understand it was not strictly required, yet flounces happen to be very fashionable this autumn, and every single dress belonging to Flossie Tulk features flounces. Possessing mine will undoubtedly help me focus more effectively on my studies. That flounce will grant me a profound sense of inner ease.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0008 }

“Having that holds some value,” Thirza conceded.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0009 }

When Miss Thorne returned to Brierley school, she discovered that every one of her students was keen to resume studying. The Regent’s class in particular prepared themselves for the battle, since at the conclusion of the approaching year, cast like a faint shadow across their road even now, towered that ominous event called “the Entrance,” a prospect that caused the hearts of each single person to plunge into their boots. What if they failed? It was a question that would torment Nell during her conscious moments throughout that winter, not excepting Sunday afternoons, driving out nearly every ethical and religious matter. Whenever Nell suffered nightmares, she saw herself gazing wretchedly at Entrance examination pass lists that displayed Hugh Carrow’s name triumphantly at the head and lacked hers altogether.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0010 }

Yet the winter passed with gaiety, activity, happiness, and speed. Studies proved just as engaging, and competition between classes remained every bit as captivating, as in previous years. Untested, enthralling realms of unexamined learning, alongside novel spheres of intellect, emotion, and aspiration, appeared to unfold in front of Nell’s enthusiastic eyes.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0011 }

“Peaks glimpsed past peak, and mountain ranges mounted upon mountain ranges.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0012 }

A great deal of this resulted from the tactful, attentive, and open-minded direction of Miss Thorne. Encouraging her students to reflect, investigate, and uncover things on their own, she promoted departing from traditional ways to an extent that thoroughly appalled Mrs. Sowerby and the school trustees, who regarded any departures from accepted practices with considerable skepticism.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0013 }

In addition to her academic pursuits Nell broadened her social life, because Thirza, keeping in mind the Tullyvale doctor’s advice, ceased forbidding the occasional excursion. Expanding successfully, the Debating Club hosted a number of concerts; a couple of parties took place that nearly resembled adult gatherings; and there was no shortage of skating outings and sleigh rides.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0014 }

In the intervals, Nell developed, sprouting so quickly that Thirza was amazed on a certain day, while they were positioned next to each other, to discover the girl surpassed her in height.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0015 }

“Why, Nell, how you’ve grown!” she uttered, in near disbelief. The statement was succeeded by a sigh. Thirza experienced a strange grief regarding Nell’s height. The young girl she had come to adore had disappeared in some manner, and replacing her was this long-limbed, grave-eyed fifteen-year-old youth possessing contemplative brows and a proudly balanced small head. Thirza adored the girl no less than she had adored the child, yet she recognized a strange, mournful feeling of bereavement. And later that evening, after Nell had departed for prayer meeting accompanied by Isolde, Thirza remained solitary in the cold dusk and surrendered to the frail indulgence of weeping. Obed, entering with a lantern, discovered her doing so and stared at her with such dismay that Thirza was compelled to laugh amid her tears.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0016 }

“My thoughts were on Nell,” she clarified. “She has grown into such a large girl—and it is likely she will be separated from us during the coming winter. Missing her will be terrible for me.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0017 }

“She’ll be in a position to return home frequently,” offered Obed in consolation, for whom Nell was still and ever would remain the tiny, enthusiastic girl he had transported home from Alder River during that June evening four years earlier. “By then, the branch railroad will have been constructed to Delford.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0018 }

“Having her in this place constantly will not be matched by it,” Thirza breathed with a sigh of gloom, resolute in her choice to indulge in her sorrow's richness without solace. “Yet there it is—such matters are beyond the comprehension of men!”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0019 }

Nell underwent additional alterations that were just as genuine as her physical transformation. To begin with, she grew far more taciturn. It is possible that her thoughts deepened and her dreaming remained just as frequent, yet her speech undoubtedly diminished. Thirza observed this as well and made remarks about it.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0020 }

“Nell, you fail to talk nearly as much as you formerly did, nor do you employ half the large words. What has happened to you?”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0021 }

As she let her book fall and gazed absently through the glass, where large, plump crimson buds were unfurling on the climbing vine, drawn forth by the enticing warmth of the spring sun, Nell blushed and gave a soft laugh.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0022 }

“I don’t know—I don’t want to talk as much,” she said, pressing a thoughtful dimple into her chin with her index finger. “It’s nicer to hold sweet, lovely thoughts quietly inside one’s heart, like treasures. I dislike having people laugh at them or marvel over them. And for some reason I don’t feel like using long words anymore. Isn't it almost a shame, now that I am actually old enough to use them if I wished to. Being nearly an adult is enjoyable in certain respects, but it isn't the sort of enjoyment I anticipated, Thirza. There are so many things to learn, accomplish, and reflect upon that no time remains for long words. Furthermore, Miss Thorne tells us that brief words possess far more strength and value. She obliges us to compose every essay we write in the simplest way we can. It proved difficult in the beginning. I had grown so accustomed to stuffing in every grand, long word I could recall—and I recalled a great many of them. However, I have grown accustomed to the practice now, and I realize how much superior it is.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0023 }

“Where is your story club these days? It has been a while since I heard you mention it.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0024 }

“Our story club has been dissolved. We lacked the time to keep it going—and besides, I believe we were growing weary of it. Composing tales of love, murder, elopements, and mysteries was foolish. Miss Thorne occasionally assigns us a story to practice our composition skills, though she restricts our writing strictly to events that could realistically occur in Brierley within our own experiences, and she evaluates our work with great severity while forcing us to evaluate our own as well. It had never occurred to me that my compositions contained such a vast number of errors until I started seeking them out on my own. My embarrassment was so deep that I wished to quit completely, yet Miss Thorne stated that I was capable of learning to write skillfully if I simply conditioned myself to act as my own harshest critic. Consequently, I am attempting to do that.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0025 }

“Just two months remain until the Entrance,” Thirza remarked. “Do you believe you can pass?”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0026 }

Nell shivered.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0027 }

“Uncertainty fills me. At times I believe I will manage—yet suddenly I become terrified. Despite our diligent studying and Miss Thorne’s rigorous drills, we still might not succeed. Every one of us faces a hurdle. My obstacle is naturally geometry, whereas Odette struggles with Latin, Opal and Wilfred find algebra troublesome, and Flossie is hindered by arithmetic. A feeling in his bones tells Elias Purdy that he will fail English history. To give us a realistic sense of what to expect, Miss Thorne plans to administer June exams that will be fully as difficult as the Entrance and graded with equal severity. How I long for it to be finished, Thirza. The thought pursues me constantly. There are nights when I awake and ponder my course of action should I fail.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0028 }

“Why, attend school the following year and give it another shot,” Thirza stated indifferently.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0029 }

“Oh, I feel I would lack the courage for that. Failing would bring so much shame, particularly if Hughie—if the rest succeeded. Furthermore, my anxiety during a test is so severe that I am prone to ruining it. I desire to possess composure similar to Odette Pullen. She remains completely unshakeable.”
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0030 }

Nell uttered a sigh and, pulling her gaze away from the enchantments of the springtime realm, the inviting day filled with wind and sky, and the sprouting green plants in the yard, firmly absorbed herself in her reading. Future springs were bound to come, yet Nell was certain that failing to get through the Entrance would leave her so devastated that she could not take pleasure in them ever again.
{: #nw-v01-c31-p0031 }
